claims.text: Chemical short-range order at nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces governs creep deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Interfacial short-range order governs creep by modifying local dislocation nucleation and mobility.
As-deposited FCC/BCC HEA multilayers have relatively random or low-SRO interfaces.
Post-deposition annealing can systematically modify SRO within the FCC and BCC layers while preserving the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
Intermediate-to-elevated temperatures under sustained loading promote dislocation-mediated creep deformation.
Changing chemical SRO at FCC/BCC interfaces modulates dislocation-interface interactions.
Enhanced interfacial SRO alters the local energy landscape for dislocation nucleation and mobility.
High interfacial SRO may act as a dislocation barrier or alter dislocation-climb processes.
Changing dislocation nucleation, mobility, or climb through SRO will change the creep rate relative to a low-SRO baseline.
Annealed multilayers with higher interfacial SRO contrast will exhibit a measurable change in creep rate and/or dislocation density and distribution relative to unannealed multilayers.
If SRO acts as an effective barrier, increased interfacial SRO will reduce creep rate and produce a different activation energy.
The as-deposited low-SRO multilayer baseline has creep governed by conventional dislocation-climb mechanisms.
Layer coarsening or phase separation caused by annealing would prevent isolation of an SRO-specific mechanism.
Lattice distortion and compositional gradients may compete with or dominate the proposed SRO effect.
A verified change in SRO accompanied by no statistically significant change in creep rate, activation energy, or dislocation-interface interactions would falsify the proposed governing role of SRO.
